channel.description: Recent content in hokkaido on Japan Specialty Traveler

item.title: Abashiri Drift Ice Guide: Icebreaker Cruises & Best Time (Feb)
item.description: Each deep winter, the Sea of Okhotsk delivers one of Japan’s most extraordinary natural spectacles to northeast Hokkaido: drift ice (ryūhyō). Vast floes of pack ice — formed far to the north and carried south on the current — crowd the coast around Abashiri and the Shiretoko Peninsula, turning the sea white to the horizon. Visitors get out among it on red icebreaker cruise ships that crunch through the floes, or by ice-walking in a dry suit.

item.title: Akan, Mashu & Kussharo Guide: Eastern Hokkaido Caldera Lakes
item.description: The remote interior of eastern Hokkaido cradles a trio of magnificent caldera lakes within Akan-Mashu National Park — a landscape of crater lakes, volcanoes, steaming earth and deep forest. Lake Akan is famous for its rare spherical marimo algae and a lively onsen town with an Ainu kotan; Lake Mashu is one of the world’s clearest lakes, often wrapped in an ethereal mist; and vast Lake Kussharo offers free lakeside hot springs and sweeping caldera views.

item.title: Asahikawa Winter Festival Guide: Snow Sculptures & Zoo
item.description: Hokkaido’s second city, Asahikawa, is one of Japan’s coldest places — and it embraces winter wholeheartedly. Each February, the Asahikawa Winter Festival raises some of the largest snow sculptures in Japan (it has held world records), with huge snow stages, slides and illuminations along the Ishikari River and downtown. The city is also home to the wildly popular Asahiyama Zoo, famous for its winter penguin walk, and is a hub for Asahikawa-style soy ramen and a gateway to the Daisetsuzan mountains.

item.title: Daisetsuzan National Park Guide: Hiking, Ropeway & Autumn
item.description: Daisetsuzan is the vast, wild roof of Hokkaido — the island’s largest national park, sometimes called “the playground of the gods” by the Ainu. A sprawling massif of volcanic peaks, alpine meadows, gorges and hot springs, it centres on Asahidake, Hokkaido’s highest mountain (2,291 m). A ropeway whisks visitors into the high country for easy boardwalk strolls or serious hikes, and each September the park lights up with Japan’s earliest autumn colours.

item.title: Furano & Biei Guide: Flower Fields, Hills & Best Time
item.description: In central Hokkaido, Furano and Biei are the postcard image of the island’s countryside — a gently rolling patchwork of fields that ripple to the horizon beneath big skies and distant mountains. Furano is famous for its summer flower fields, above all the purple sweep of lavender, while neighbouring Biei enchants with sculpted hills, lone trees and the surreal Blue Pond. Whether you drive the panorama roads, cycle the lanes or ride the seasonal train, this is one of Japan’s most beautiful rural landscapes.

item.title: Furano Lavender Guide: Best Time, Farms & Festival (Jul)
item.description: For a few glorious weeks each July, the hills around Furano turn purple as Hokkaido’s famous lavender fields come into bloom — one of Japan’s great summer sights. Rows of fragrant lavender sweep toward the mountains, joined by rainbow ribbons of poppies, salvia and marigolds, all under crisp northern skies. The legendary Farm Tomita leads a cluster of flower farms offering viewing, lavender soft cream and sweets, picking experiences and festivals.

item.title: Hakodate Christmas Fantasy Guide: Dates, Lights & Access
item.description: Each December, Hakodate’s romantic bayfront glows for Hakodate Christmas Fantasy — a festive waterfront event built around a giant illuminated Christmas tree floating in the harbour. Set against the historic Kanemori Red Brick Warehouses and reflected in the water, the tree (a gift tradition linked to sister-city Halifax) is joined by sparkling illuminations, a nightly light-up “moment,” soup kitchens with hot food, and even fireworks. Combined with Hakodate’s world-famous night view from the mountain, it makes the city a magical place to be in early winter.

item.title: Hakodate Guide: Night View, Morning Market & Access
item.description: A historic port at Hokkaido’s southern tip, Hakodate was one of Japan’s first cities opened to foreign trade, and it wears that heritage beautifully. The headline attraction is the night view from Mt. Hakodate — the glittering, hourglass-shaped cityscape pinched between two bays, rated among Japan’s finest. By day, dig into the bustling morning market for the freshest crab, uni and squid-on-rice, wander the European-flavoured Motomachi slopes, and admire the star-shaped Goryokaku fort.

item.title: Hokkaido Bear Watching Guide: Where & How to See Brown Bears
item.description: Hokkaido is home to the Ezo brown bear (higuma), Japan’s largest land animal, plus a rich cast of northern wildlife — deer, red foxes, Steller’s sea eagles, red-crowned cranes and whales. Seeing a wild brown bear is a genuine thrill, and Hokkaido offers some of Japan’s best opportunities to do so safely and responsibly, above all from boat cruises along the Shiretoko coast where bears forage on the shore. For guaranteed sightings, well-run bear parks let families get close.

item.title: Hokkaido Salmon Fishing Guide: Rivers, Season & Tours
item.description: Salmon are woven into Hokkaido’s culture, cuisine and seasons, and autumn brings one of nature’s great spectacles to the island: the salmon run, when chum and pink salmon surge back from the sea to spawn in the rivers where they were born. For anglers, Hokkaido offers superb shore (surf) and river fishing; for everyone else, watching thousands of salmon battle upstream — or visiting a hatchery and the Sapporo Salmon Museum — is unforgettable.

item.title: Hokkaido Snowshoe Guide: Forest Tours, Season & Tips
item.description: For a peaceful, accessible way to experience Hokkaido’s magical winter, strap on snowshoes and walk out into the silent, snow-laden forest. Snowshoeing lets you float over deep powder that would swallow ordinary boots, following guides into birch woods, frozen wetlands and national-park trails far from the crowds. No experience is needed — if you can walk, you can snowshoe — making it perfect for families and first-time winter adventurers. Look for animal tracks, frost-covered trees and frozen waterfalls, and warm up afterwards in an onsen.

item.title: Jingisukan Guide: Hokkaido's Grilled Lamb BBQ & Where to Eat
item.description: Jingisukan (“Genghis Khan”) is Hokkaido’s beloved grilled-mutton barbecue, a smoky, sociable feast named for the dome-shaped grill said to resemble a warrior’s helmet. Diners cook lamb or mutton and a pile of vegetables — onions, beansprouts, cabbage, pumpkin — over the convex iron grill, where juices run down to flavour the veg around the rim. Washed down with ice-cold beer in a summer beer garden or a lively grill house, it’s one of Hokkaido’s most fun and convivial meals.

item.title: Lake Toya Guide: Showa Shinzan, Onsen & Access
item.description: Lake Toya (Toyako) is a serene, near-circular caldera lake in southwest Hokkaido, ringed by gentle hills and watched over by a pair of very active volcanoes — the lava dome of Showa Shinzan (which rose from a wheat field in the 1940s) and Mt. Usu. A UNESCO Global Geopark, the area pairs lakeside hot-spring resorts with dramatic volcanic scenery, ropeway views, and — every night through the long summer — a fireworks display over the water.

item.title: Niseko Guide: Skiing, Powder Snow & Season
item.description: Niseko is Japan’s most famous ski destination and a global byword for powder snow. Blessed with extraordinarily light, abundant “Japow” blown in off the Sea of Japan, this resort area on the flank of Mt. Niseko Annupuri — gazing across to the perfect cone of Mt. Yotei — draws skiers and snowboarders from around the world. Four interconnected ski areas, lively après-ski, world-class dining and superb onsen make it a winter resort like no other, while summer brings rafting, cycling and hiking in cool mountain air.

item.title: Noboribetsu Onsen Guide: Jigokudani, Baths & Access
item.description: Noboribetsu is Hokkaido’s most famous hot-spring resort, and one of the best in all Japan. Its power source is Jigokudani (“Hell Valley”) — a dramatic, steaming crater of sulphurous vents, bubbling streams and rust-coloured rock that feeds the town’s baths. Noboribetsu is prized for the sheer variety of its waters — nine different spring types in one place — so ryokan and day-use bathhouses offer a soak for every ailment. Easy from Sapporo or on the road to Hakodate, it’s a quintessential Hokkaido onsen experience.

item.title: Otaru Guide: Canal, Glassworks & Day Trip from Sapporo
item.description: A short train ride from Sapporo, Otaru is a postcard-pretty port town built on a once-booming herring and trade economy. Its centrepiece is the Otaru Canal, lined with handsome stone warehouses and Victorian-style gas lamps — impossibly romantic at dusk and magical under winter snow. The old merchant streets now brim with glassblowing studios, music-box shops, sushi counters and sake breweries. Easy to reach and full of charm, Otaru is one of Hokkaido’s most popular day trips.

item.title: Sapporo Autumn Fest Guide: Hokkaido Food Festival (Sep)
item.description: Every September, Odori Park fills with the smells of grilling seafood, sizzling meat and fresh produce for the Sapporo Autumn Fest (Sapporo Autumn Festival) — a glorious celebration of Hokkaido’s harvest and one of Japan’s great food events. For several weeks, the park’s blocks become themed gourmet zones showcasing the bounty of the island: crab and scallops, ramen, jingisukan, soup curry, dairy, sweets, sake and local wine, region by region. With long tables, autumn weather and the whole island’s cuisine in one place, it’s a food lover’s dream and a delicious way to round off summer.

item.title: Sapporo Beer Garden Guide: Museum, Beer Hall & Summer
item.description: Sapporo is the birthplace of Japanese beer, and the Sapporo Beer Garden is the place to toast it. Set in a handsome red-brick complex that once brewed the nation’s beer, the site pairs the only Beer Museum in Japan with grand beer halls where the classic Hokkaido feast — all-you-can-eat jingisukan (grilled lamb) with all-you-can-drink beer — has been served for generations. In summer, the city throws an even bigger party: a vast open-air beer garden takes over Odori Park.

item.title: Sapporo Guide: Odori Park, Susukino & Things to Do
item.description: Sapporo, Hokkaido’s vibrant capital and Japan’s fifth-largest city, is the gateway to the north and a destination in its own right. Laid out on an easy American-style grid, it centres on the long green ribbon of Odori Park, runs north to the historic Clock Tower and former government buildings, and south into the neon buzz of Susukino, one of Japan’s great nightlife and dining districts. Add legendary food — miso ramen, soup curry, jingisukan and crab — plus year-round festivals, and Sapporo is the perfect base for exploring Hokkaido.

item.title: Sapporo Ramen Guide: Miso Ramen, Best Shops & How to Eat
item.description: Sapporo is the birthplace of miso ramen, one of Japan’s three great ramen styles — and a bowl built for Hokkaido winters. Rich, hearty and warming, it pairs a deep miso-based pork broth with thick, curly yellow noodles, a slick of lard to keep it piping hot, and toppings like sweetcorn, butter, beansprouts and chashu. Slurping a steaming bowl in a tiny counter shop while snow falls outside is a classic Hokkaido moment.

item.title: Sapporo Snow Festival Guide: Dates, Sites & Tips (Feb)
item.description: The Sapporo Snow Festival (Yuki Matsuri) is Japan’s biggest and most famous winter event, drawing millions to Hokkaido’s capital each February. For about a week, Odori Park becomes a glittering open-air gallery of colossal snow sculptures — towering castles, temples and pop-culture characters — alongside delicate ice sculptures in Susukino and a family snow-play zone at the Tsudome. After dark, the sculptures are spectacularly lit up and projection-mapped. With street food, hot drinks and a magical atmosphere, it’s a bucket-list winter experience.

item.title: Sapporo Soup Curry Guide: What It Is & Where to Eat
item.description: Soup curry is a Sapporo original and one of Hokkaido’s most addictive dishes — a fragrant, spiced, brothy curry that’s worlds apart from the thick Japanese curry-rice found elsewhere. A light but deeply flavoured soup, often built on chicken or seafood stock and a blend of spices, comes brimming with big chunks of Hokkaido vegetables — pumpkin, lotus root, peppers, broccoli — and a hero protein like fall-off-the-bone chicken leg. You choose your spice level and eat it by dipping spoonfuls of rice into the soup.

item.title: Shakotan Peninsula Guide: Cape Kamui, Blue Sea & Uni
item.description: West of Otaru, the rugged Shakotan Peninsula is famous for one thing above all: the colour of its sea. The vivid, jewel-like “Shakotan Blue” glows beneath dramatic cliffs and capes, making this one of Hokkaido’s most beautiful stretches of coast and its only marine park. Walk out to wild Cape Kamui and Cape Shimamui for sweeping ocean views, then feast on the region’s celebrated summer sea urchin (uni), served gloriously fresh on rice.

item.title: Shiretoko Peninsula Guide: UNESCO Nature, Cruises & Bears
item.description: Jutting into the Sea of Okhotsk at Hokkaido’s far northeast, the Shiretoko Peninsula is one of Japan’s last great wildernesses — a UNESCO World Heritage site where primeval forest, volcanic peaks and a wild coast of cliffs and waterfalls shelter an extraordinary density of wildlife. This is brown bear country, home also to deer, foxes, eagles and, offshore, whales and seals. Explore the Shiretoko Five Lakes, take a nature cruise beneath sea cliffs, and in late winter watch drift ice pack the shore.

item.title: Tokachi Millennium Forest Guide: Gardens, Tickets & Access
item.description: In the rolling countryside of the Tokachi plain lies the Tokachi Millennium Forest, one of Japan’s most celebrated contemporary gardens. Conceived as a 1,000-year project to reconnect people with nature, it blends manicured garden artistry with the wild Hokkaido landscape — most famously the sculpted, wave-like grass mounds of the Earth Garden and the lush perennial borders of the Meadow Garden, designed by acclaimed plantsman Piet Oudolf. An international garden-design award-winner, it’s a serene, beautiful stop, with goats, cafés, cycling and forest trails to enjoy at a gentle pace.

item.title: Upopoy Ainu Museum Guide: Tickets, Highlights & Access
item.description: Upopoy (the National Ainu Museum and Park) at Shiraoi is Japan’s flagship centre for the culture of the Ainu, the Indigenous people of Hokkaido and the north. Opened in 2020 on the shore of Lake Poroto, this thoughtful complex tells the Ainu story — their language, beliefs, crafts and connection to nature — long marginalised and now celebrated. With a modern museum, traditional houses, live music and dance, craft demonstrations and hands-on workshops, Upopoy is a moving, eye-opening stop that adds real depth to a Hokkaido trip.

item.title: Yoichi Nikka Whisky Distillery Guide: Tour, Tasting & Access
item.description: The Yoichi Nikka Whisky Distillery, on the coast just beyond Otaru, is the birthplace of one of Japan’s most storied whiskies — and a pilgrimage for whisky lovers. Founded in 1934 by Masataka Taketsuru, “the father of Japanese whisky,” who chose Yoichi for its Scotland-like climate, the distillery still uses traditional coal-fired pot stills. The handsome stone-and-ivy grounds (the setting of a famous NHK drama) house the working distillery, a whisky museum and a tasting bar.

item.title: Yosakoi Soran Festival Guide: Dates, Where to Watch & Access
item.description: Every June, Sapporo explodes with colour, music and motion for the Yosakoi Soran Festival — one of Japan’s most exhilarating dance events. Hundreds of teams, tens of thousands of dancers in bold costumes, surge through the streets and across stages, naruko clappers in hand, to powerful remixes of Hokkaido’s traditional “Soran Bushi” fishing song. Born only in 1992, the festival fuses Kochi’s yosakoi dance with Hokkaido’s sea-shanty heritage into a thrilling, modern spectacle that fills Odori Park and the city for several days.

item.title: Best Hotels & Ryokan in Hokkaido: Where to Stay in 2026
item.description: Hokkaido’s vast geography — 83,000 km², roughly the size of Austria — means accommodation strategy varies dramatically by destination. Sapporo offers urban hotel convenience; Niseko delivers world-class ski resort lodging; and the onsen towns of Noboribetsu and Jozankei provide some of Japan’s finest hot spring ryokan experiences. Best Areas to Stay in Hokkaido Sapporo — Best Hub for All Seasons Japan’s fifth-largest city. Excellent restaurants, the Sapporo Snow Festival in February, and train access to many Hokkaido highlights.

item.title: Hokkaido Family Trip: Snow Activities, Farms, Bears & Kid-Friendly Hokkaido
item.description: Hokkaido offers something that Japan’s urban destinations cannot: space and nature at a scale that makes sense to children. An animal walking toward you in the wild, a penguin that passes at eye level on a bridge, a dairy farm where you watch a cow being milked and drink the milk 30 minutes later — these experiences have a directness that theme park rides approximate but cannot replicate. This guide covers Hokkaido’s family-specific attractions with practical detail on what works for different age groups.

item.title: Hokkaido Festivals 2026: Sapporo Snow Festival, Yosakoi Soran & Lavender
item.description: Hokkaido’s festivals are as seasonal as its landscape — in winter, ice and snow; in spring, flowers; in summer, lavender and beer; in autumn, harvest and cranes. The key distinction from festivals elsewhere in Japan is scale: the Sapporo Snow Festival’s main sculptures are built by the Japan Self-Defence Forces using military engineering equipment, and the Yosakoi Soran festival deploys 30,000 dancers across a city. This guide covers the major events with specific advice on what most visitors miss and how to experience each festival beyond the standard tourist circuit.

item.title: Hokkaido Food Guide: Crab, Uni, Soup Curry, Ramen & Dairy
item.description: Hokkaido’s food culture has an unusual characteristic for Japan: it is genuinely young. The island’s large-scale settlement began in the 1870s, which means its food traditions are 150 years old — not the centuries-old layered cuisine of Kyoto or the Edo period’s Tokyo. This created a food culture that is simultaneously Japanese and something else: lamb barbecue borrowed from sheep-farming experiments, soup curry developed in a pharmacy consultation, ramen styles refined from scratch in the post-war decades, and dairy that exists because American agricultural advisors arrived in 1870 and told Hokkaido to become the dairy region of Japan.

item.title: Hokkaido Girls' Trip: Dairy Sweets, Otaru Romance & Lavender Fields
item.description: Hokkaido’s appeal for a girls' trip is different from Kyoto’s kimono-and-temple aesthetic or Tokyo’s shopping circuit — it operates on the level of landscape, dairy, and a slower pace that the southern islands rarely permit. The flower fields genuinely are as beautiful as the photographs suggest; the soft-serve ice cream made from milk that arrived from a farm that morning is a materially different object from anything sold in Tokyo; and the onsen ryokan experience in Noboribetsu or Jozankei has a depth of tradition that justifies being the trip’s centrepiece rather than an add-on.

item.title: Hokkaido Hidden Gems: Shakotan Blue Coast, Tomamu Ice Village & Beyond
item.description: Hokkaido’s tourist circuit — Sapporo, Otaru, Hakodate, Niseko, Furano — is genuinely excellent. But the island is the size of Austria, and the tourist circuit covers perhaps 5% of its geography. The remaining 95% includes a peninsula with water colour found only in the Mediterranean and Okinawa, an ice hotel that is rebuilt entirely every winter in a mountain valley, a bankrupt city that reinvented itself around a single piece of fruit, and Japan’s most underrated industrial night view.

item.title: Hokkaido Honeymoon Guide: Lavender Ryokan, Private Onsen & Mountain Scenery
item.description: Hokkaido’s honeymoon appeal rests on three things that other Japanese destinations cannot offer simultaneously: genuinely wild landscape, private onsen bathing, and a seasonal extreme — whether summer lavender fields or winter powder snow — that transforms the scenery into something specific to the time of year. The island also has the practical advantage of scale: the distance between destinations creates a sense of genuine travel rather than movement between tourist sites, and the long drives through the Tokachi plains or along the Shiretoko coast have a quality of space that contributes to the trip’s atmosphere.

item.title: Hokkaido Mystery Guide: Escape Rooms, Goryokaku's Last Republic & Ainu Secrets
item.description: Hokkaido’s mysteries operate at an unusual intersection of the very recent (150 years of recorded colonial history) and the very ancient (10,000+ years of Ainu culture that the colonisation systematically attempted to erase). The island’s short institutional history means the historical record is remarkably complete — Enomoto Takeaki’s Republic of Ezo lasted less than a year and is documented in extraordinary detail — while the Ainu cultural codes embedded in Hokkaido’s landscape names have only recently begun to be properly interpreted.

item.title: Hokkaido Nature Guide: Shiretoko, Daisetsuzan, Furano & Kushiro
item.description: Hokkaido’s nature operates on a scale that Japan’s other islands cannot match. The island is 83,000 square kilometres — roughly the size of Austria — and contains 6 national parks, including Japan’s largest (Daisetsuzan) and one of its two UNESCO World Heritage natural sites (Shiretoko). The wildlife is genuinely wild: brown bears that fish for salmon in rivers accessible from the road, red-crowned cranes that are among the world’s rarest birds, and an autumn foliage season that begins 3–4 weeks before the rest of Japan.

item.title: Hokkaido Sightseeing: Sapporo, Hakodate, Otaru & Beyond
item.description: Hokkaido’s sightseeing does not fit the standard Japan template. The island was only formally incorporated into the Japanese state in 1869 — before that, it was Ainu territory supplemented by a small number of Matsumae Domain outposts. The colonial infrastructure (kaitaku, development) was built in the Meiji era with American agricultural advisors and a European city-planning sensibility that gives Sapporo its wide boulevards and Hakodate its Western hillside district. The result is a Japan that feels different at a structural level — more space, a younger built environment, and a relationship with the land that reflects 150 years of active settlement rather than 1,500 years of layered culture.

item.title: Hokkaido Ski Guide: Niseko, Furano, Rusutsu & Backcountry Powder
item.description: Hokkaido’s skiing has a global reputation built on a single physical fact: the combination of cold Siberian air masses crossing the Sea of Japan and Hokkaido’s volcanic terrain produces the driest, lightest powder snow on earth. Skiers call it “Japow” — a portmanteau that has become an international brand for the conditions that Niseko, Furano, and a dozen smaller resorts deliver consistently from December through March. This guide covers the major resorts with specific guidance on where the crowds are, where the powder actually is, and what the backcountry options involve for intermediate to advanced skiers.

item.title: Hokkaido Solo Travel Guide: Cycling, Hiking, Seafood Counters & Wild Camping
item.description: Solo travel in Hokkaido rewards a specific kind of independence — the willingness to drive an empty road for two hours toward a peninsula that has nothing in particular except the shape of the land and the sea. Hokkaido doesn’t have a dense tourist circuit with comfortable stops every 30 minutes. The island’s tourism infrastructure follows a few well-worn tracks, and outside those tracks the infrastructure thins rapidly. This is not a liability for solo travellers — it is the reason to come.

item.title: Best Ramen in Sapporo: A Local's Guide
item.description: Best Ramen in Sapporo: A Locals Guide to Hokkaido’s Soul-Warming Bowl If you’ve ever slurped a bowl of ramen in Tokyo or Osaka and thought, “This is as good as it gets,” I need you to reconsider. Because Sapporo — Hokkaido’s snow-dusted, food-obsessed capital — is where ramen transcends from a quick meal into something approaching a spiritual experience. This best ramen in Sapporo locals guide exists because, after living in Japan for 15 years and making more trips to Hokkaido than I can count, I’m convinced that Sapporo is the single greatest ramen city in the entire country.

item.title: Hokkaido Lavender Season in Furano Summer 2026
item.description: Hokkaido Lavender Season in Furano: When to Visit for the Perfect Purple Panorama (2024–2025 Guide) Introduction: Why Summer in Hokkaido Is Japan’s Best-Kept Secret Every July, while the rest of Japan swelters under oppressive humidity and 35°C heat, something magical happens in central Hokkaido. Rolling hills explode into ribbons of purple, violet, and white as lavender fields reach their fragrant peak — and the entire Furano-Kamifurano region transforms into what feels like a slice of Provence dropped into the Japanese countryside.

item.title: Hokkaido Winter 2026 Snow Festivals & Skiing Guide
item.description: Hokkaido Winter Travel Guide: Snow Festivals, Skiing, and the Best Regional Food in Japan’s Northern Frontier There’s a moment I experience every winter that reminds me why I fell in love with Hokkaido. It’s late January, and I’m standing on the edge of Odori Park in Sapporo at dusk. The snow sculptures — some of them five stories tall — are just beginning to glow under colored lights, and the air is so cold it catches in your throat.

item.title: Hokkaido Winter 2026: Snow Festivals Travel Guide
item.description: Hokkaido Winter Travel Guide: Snow Festivals, Powder Snow & the Best Regional Cuisine in Japan’s Northern Frontier There is a moment, standing in the blue twilight of a February evening in Sapporo, when the massive ice sculptures of the Yuki Matsuri begin to glow from within, and the cold bites your cheeks, and the smell of grilled lamb drifts from a nearby yatai stall — that is when you understand why millions of visitors brave sub-zero temperatures to come here every year.
